title: Preacceleration, passive restraint and retrofit compression
construction: The interview describes a two-X44 intake at 2.5:1, passive carbon upper roller, roller-floor transmission described as 17:19, and a 3-inch steel drum driven by four X60s with powered hood rollers. A previously powered upper feed roller was made passive after jamming. Drum-region compression is reported as 3/8 inch and final roller compression as 1/2 inch.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly connects the stepped compression to fitting a replacement shooter in the existing robot, and the passive roller change to avoiding fuel being driven downward into jams. Collector repair access is deliberate because it receives impacts.
engineering_analysis: The important reference is the sequence of contacts, not simply four launcher motors. Upstream acceleration reduces the velocity increment demanded of the drum, while the passive restraint prevents one contact from injecting fuel into an already occupied region. More powered surfaces can therefore lower useful flow. A retrofit also fixes the available path length and elevation; its compression distribution cannot safely be transplanted without the same incoming velocity and support geometry. Separately, the agitation priority hierarchy means collector deployment and automatic shooting agitation are competing commands rather than independent subsystems.
recommended_validation: Measure hopper-to-exit rate and current with the upper restraint passive versus driven, at several fill levels. Check worn fuel and simultaneous agitation. Preserve the source ratio order until driver/driven orientation is verified.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Dish packaging and shooting independence require a coordinated robot
construction: The interview describes an eleven-position dish, front and rear vertical roller sets to clear its center, approximately 425 degrees of turret freedom, a 3-inch main shooter wheel, a 1-inch upper roller and additional feed wheels. A third X44 was added for difficult passes and corner shots. Intake and drivetrain packaging are shaped around the large dish.
team_stated_reason: The team identifies moving shots, shooting under defense and simultaneous acquisition as reasons to retain the turret architecture. The doubled vertical rollers address fuel left in the dish center; the extra shooter motor addresses range/power demand.
engineering_analysis: A centrally packaged turret is a whole-robot commitment. The dish determines where modules, structure and storage can sit, and its useful capacity depends on clearing the central dead region rather than nominal perimeter volume. Turret range is only useful if localization, target selection, hood travel and cable management support it. The FMS-aware timing offset is a flight-time decision: fuel released before activation must arrive while scoring is valid. That offset is not a transferable constant without checking release-to-arrival time and the applicable game timing.
recommended_validation: Compare central residual fuel, sustained rate and moving-shot accuracy at different turret angles. Validate the hub-state lead time against measured flight time; verify cable/swept-volume clearance over the claimed angular range.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A rising fuel path makes agitation and service mass consequential
construction: The collector kicker changed from a hanging deployed bar to a member that folds with the hopper. Side agitation, passive dead-zone rollers, added gripping rollers and a belt-linked roller elevator feed the drum. The retained dated source account records the climber being installed March 1 and removed March 19 before the first event.
team_stated_reason: The folding kicker is explained as improving bump clearance. Added contact surfaces respond to trapped fuel and insufficient feed. The retained team account attributes removing the climber to weight, with later mass devoted to reliable feeding.
engineering_analysis: This design transports fuel upward before release, so every additional elevation change has a traction and packing cost. An apparently small passive roller may be important because it removes a place where the moving stream can unload into a dead pocket. The coupled hopper/kicker motion is also a route-clearance feature, not merely storage expansion. Removing a climber should be understood as reallocating mass and development effort to the bottleneck; it does not imply that tower scoring was mechanically impossible or that endgame fuel should be counted as climb value.
recommended_validation: Log current and residual inventory along the entire rising path, test folding while fully loaded, and compare bump clearance before and after the kicker folds. Do not derive undisclosed gear ratios from the interview wording.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Protected carbon intake and continuous J-path launcher feed
construction: A 2×1 aluminum crash member protects a carbon intake roller. Later wrist plates use half-inch stock with raised hard-stop contact regions and pocketing. The shooter uses a J-shaped accelerating tunnel, a separate feeder, a four-X60 steel drum and powered hood rollers; its hood pivot is supported independently of the drum. Two side cameras were added to the original front Limelight.
team_stated_reason: The team links the crash member to allowing a light but impact-sensitive roller, larger hard-stop contact to reduced wear, low electronics/wiring to a lower floor, and additional cameras to midfield vision gaps found at Half Moon Bay. The source also describes replacing an earlier S-shaped path after direction reversal hurt consistency.
engineering_analysis: The useful package combines structural load routing with flow continuity. The crash member must intercept contact before the carbon roller does; copying only the carbon tube removes the condition that made it practical. A lower floor reduces the climb imposed on loose fuel, while a J-path avoids reversing the velocity component that was just created upstream. Independent hood support can reduce parasitic coupling, but hood and drum still need controlled compression over their complete angle range. The camera change is evidence that good scoring performance near the hub did not guarantee adequate pose observability in midfield.
recommended_validation: Measure path velocity and compression through hood travel, inspect crash loads with the collector extended, and compare localization availability in midfield before and after adding side views. Retain a separate shooter-ready gate before enabling the floor.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Precondition fuel before a compact turret, then manage defended stability
construction: The interview describes eleven active carbon/silicone floor rollers powered by an X60 through a stated 2:1 reduction, with 3-mm-pitch GT2 inter-roller belts. A later acceleration stage is described as delivering approximately 8 m/s with near-zero incoming spin. Compact turret packaging shares shafts and places hood-drive hardware to limit diameter. A defended shooting mode cancels shooting on the move.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly cites efficiency at small pulley radii for its belt choice and compactness for the turret transmission layout. Its defended mode is explained as planting the robot to resist being pushed and emptying more accurately.
engineering_analysis: Preconditioning is a useful way to separate high-volume transport from precision release. A turret receiving fuel with controlled velocity and spin needs to add less correction, but it inherits errors in every upstream roller and transfer gap. The reported 8 m/s is an internal-stage claim, not a measured final trajectory specification or match-average rate. A planted mode also shows why turret capability does not require moving continuously: the best control mode depends on contact conditions. A future implementation must budget traction and battery demand for both upstream acceleration and chassis resistance.
recommended_validation: Measure entrance velocity/spin distribution, current at each stage, and accuracy under controlled lateral contact. Compare planted and moving modes with the same fuel condition and load rather than ranking them from an undefended demo.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Twin spindexers trade packaging freedom for multiple coupled interfaces
construction: The mechanism has two rotating floor/cone systems and uptake ramps, separately controlled kickers, independent turrets and hood adjustment. The interview describes X44-driven indexer systems, 6-inch aluminum flywheels replacing heavy steel trials, an under-mounted battery on a pinned removable panel, and chassis-speed-dependent intake voltage bounded around 6.5–12 V.
team_stated_reason: Aluminum flywheels were chosen after the steel trial proved too heavy. The battery mounting responds to crowded internal packaging. The retained interview account describes bristles, stacked wheels and shaped cones as successive feed iterations.
engineering_analysis: Two aiming channels do not automatically double match output. Fuel must be distributed to both cones, delivered through both ramps and accelerated without one path starving or overpacking. Moving-shot math must use the location of each turret rather than a single robot-center vector; angular chassis motion creates different local velocities at separated release points. Dynamic collector speed can match acquisition to chassis motion, but the exact speed signal and interpolation should be checked in code because the caption wording mixes angular and translational quantities. The removable battery panel is part of the architecture: dense packaging is only useful if the robot can still be serviced reliably.
recommended_validation: Test unequal hopper loading, one jammed lane, low battery, turning shots and underbody battery retention after bump contact. Verify the actual intake-speed input in source code before reproducing the controller.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Rebuild removes feed compression and separates shooter readiness
construction: The interview distinguishes a former divided two-lane/double-spindexer arrangement from the drum rebuild with a roller floor. A powered lower intake roller was replaced by two 3/4-inch aluminum shafts with reduced compression. Compliant wheels near entry feed a J-shaped path; a guide was added after WPI wobble. Four motors drive the drum/kicker/hood group, and feed is enabled only after aiming, speed and hood conditions are satisfied.
team_stated_reason: The team reports improved throughput after reducing collector compression, adds the guide to control observed motion, and describes reduced belt tension as a current-draw improvement. Driver controls were intentionally simplified around repeatable actions.
engineering_analysis: This is evidence against treating maximum grip as maximum throughput. Too many opposing powered contacts can trap deformable fuel or make its entry velocity inconsistent. Removing a roller changes the entire force chain, so the improvement should not be generalized to a collector with different ground geometry. Likewise, the software shoot command is a sequencer rather than a simultaneous motor-on command. Feeding early can pull down wheel speed or create an inaccurate initial volley, while waiting unnecessarily long reduces usable shift time.
recommended_validation: Compare feed latency, initial-volley accuracy, current and residual fuel with the actual readiness tolerances. Inspect the added guide over hood travel and repeat reduced-compression tests with worn fuel.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Large inventory changes collector loading, frame clearance and drive gearing
construction: The interview reports approximately 115-fuel capacity, a 33.5×21.375-inch robot envelope before the described extension, a wide 3-inch two-X60 intake, a load shield above the collector, and hopper structure changed from angle to tube. A two-position hood changed from pneumatic to linear actuation; wheel speed covers intermediate distances. Custom modules allow ratio changes and were geared down for the loaded robot.
team_stated_reason: The second collector motor and load shield respond to stalling and hopper pressure. Tube structure responds to racking and snagging. The lower drive ratio is explicitly tied to moving a heavily loaded robot across bumps with less stalling/current; the source attributes the actuator change to weight.
engineering_analysis: Capacity is useful only if it remains mobile and unloads reliably. A large stored column presses on its lowest contact surfaces, so a shield can be more valuable than another nominally faster roller. The hopper bar cutout and wheel sizing belong to the same route-clearance problem: a robot that can collect a full load but beaches on the bump loses the strategic value of that load. Two hood positions simplify mechanism travel, but the remaining range must be supplied by speed without creating unacceptable release-angle or recovery-time sensitivity.
recommended_validation: Test acceleration, bump traversal, braking, tip margin and current at empty/half/full inventory. Measure sustained unload rate rather than dividing nominal capacity by the fastest initial volley. Verify exact dimensions and the source gear notation in CAD.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A drum rebuild shifts the problem to inertia, loading and inspection mass
construction: The interview distinguishes the former turret from a four-X60 drum rebuild. A long kicker ramp maintains contact; a stub-roller floor pivots with the collector, with a jackshaft inside a roller. Passive hopper/net expansion is reported as roughly 50–55 fuel unexpanded and up to 78 expanded. A 1.5-lb steel flywheel with a stated 1:3 transmission supplements launcher inertia. The planned L1 mechanism was removed at inspection.
team_stated_reason: The team attributes the ramp to sustained compression, the added flywheel to speed droop while feeding a large load, and climb removal to a discrepancy between shop and event weighing. A revised hood ratio sought a compromise between actuation speed and resistance to disturbance.
engineering_analysis: The supplementary flywheel stores energy in the motor-to-drum system; its contribution depends on the square of its speed ratio. That does not establish a sustained power budget, so a high first-volley rate may still decay. The pivoting floor improves access but introduces moving shaft/alignment interfaces. The source caption calls one small drum dimension ambiguously; do not infer diameter from that wording. Likewise, a removed climber is an unfielded feature for the filmed configuration, not an autonomous capability.
recommended_validation: Measure speed droop over a complete hopper and repeated shifts, verify drive/driven ratio order, and calibrate scales before allocating the final mass margin.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Surface contamination, inertia and power control interact
construction: The collector deploy angle was flattened after first-event jams. The retained interview account describes surgical tubing replaced by grippier floor surfaces after fuel debris caused slip. The shooter uses a four-X60 aluminum drum, powered upper rollers and a compact geared steel flywheel; transfer is sequenced after launcher speed is reached. Current, voltage and temperature logging inform operating limits.
team_stated_reason: The team links the added flywheel to reduced speed decay and improved end-of-hopper accuracy. Floor/collector changes respond to observed jamming and contamination, while software limiting responds to the total electrical demand.
engineering_analysis: A material choice can work with clean practice fuel yet fail when loose surface debris changes friction. A flywheel can smooth a transient without fixing an inadequate recharge rate or a hot motor. The useful design reference is therefore a tested material/contact path plus an explicit electrical budget, not a motor count. Robot logging should distinguish commanded voltage, actual bus voltage, current limit, speed error and fuel flow; otherwise starvation and electrical saturation can look like the same shooting symptom.
recommended_validation: Repeat full-hopper tests with used fuel and low batteries. Compare surface cleanliness, slip, speed recovery and motor temperature over multiple shifts rather than a single successful volley.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Passive feed solved one jam while rack durability remained unresolved
construction: The rack collector and belt floor feed an originally divided shooter that became one continuous drum. In the team’s later technical discussion, powered upper/lower indexing rollers overpacked the ramp; immobilizing the lower rollers corrected that feed issue. The static hood avoids an exposed powered-roller belt. The team separately reports repeated polycarbonate rack-tooth failures and a 45-A deploying/5-A deployed current-limit strategy at Worlds.
team_stated_reason: The stated priorities are simple, durable mechanisms and resistance to trench contact. The lower surface was made static to meter entry rather than forcing fuel into a congested ramp. The current-limit change aimed to let the intake collapse under impact; failures became less frequent but did not disappear.
engineering_analysis: This example needs two distinct failure histories. A feed-path change can be successful while the deployment structure remains unreliable. Stronger propulsion is not automatically the fix for a packing jam, and a high-performing alliance run does not certify rack durability. Source-reported storage also has a useful distinction: almost 70 geometric capacity versus commonly 50–60 in play. Protected interior PETG vector wheels surviving a season is not evidence that the same prints would survive as exposed intake wheels.
recommended_validation: Test the passive lower feed with full hopper pressure and varied fuel. Instrument deployment impact/current and inspect tooth-root damage. A proposed decoupling of intake sides is a future idea, not a fielded fix.
limitations: Focused interview plus first-party technical replies 5, 8, 11, 13 and 15 in topic 521008. Tech-slide access returned Gone; the slides were not reviewed or counted as a binder.

title: Trench access and speed-error feeding explain the rebuild
construction: A slotted three-roller transfer provides adjustable compression before a two-X60 high-inertia launcher. The flexible Hopper Flopper compresses under the trench and re-expands afterward. The shooter was reversed relative to the original robot, and the feeder speed varies with launcher speed error. The interview explicitly reports no climb.
team_stated_reason: The team links trench access to losing neutral-zone fuel races, preserving capacity to avoiding a smaller fixed hopper, and reversed orientation to reducing the need to turn after acquisition. Transfer modulation is intended to give fuel sufficient energy transfer while maintaining accuracy.
engineering_analysis: A compliant storage envelope changes which routes are available, so its value cannot be measured only in added fuel. It can change autonomous arrival order and the opponent’s available supply. Speed-error-dependent feed is a form of demand management: slow entry when the launcher is behind instead of allowing a nominally high feed command to create low-energy misses. The caption’s flywheel mass arithmetic is inconsistent, so preserve the qualitative high-inertia claim and seek a published mass breakdown rather than silently choosing one number.
recommended_validation: Compare route arrival times, full-load trench passage, recovery after contact, and total scored fuel with fixed versus variable feeding. Measure sustained and initial BPS separately.
limitations: Interview plus team replies in topic 515730. The first release reports about 15–16 BPS over a full roughly 80-fuel hopper versus around 20–25 initially; these are team reports for that configuration, not measurements of every later revision.

title: A fixed-angle launcher deliberately shifts complexity elsewhere
construction: The interview describes a passively deploying intake/hopper, roller floor explicitly inspired by 2017 team 254, a separate feed stage, a four-X60 launcher and added brass flywheel inertia. The hood is fixed; distance changes use speed and chassis aim. Intake motion agitates the stored fuel, and the aiming system has a manual fallback.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly credits the historical floor reference and identifies the fallback as a way to keep playing when automatic aim fails. No team-stated numerical optimum for fixed hood angle is established in this passage.
engineering_analysis: Removing hood actuation reduces moving hardware, but does not remove aiming requirements. The usable trajectory envelope is now constrained by wheel speed, launch angle, release height, accuracy and the routes from which the chassis can point at the target. The passive deployment also makes initial orientation and autonomous motion part of the mechanism’s operation. A simple subsystem can therefore demand careful whole-match planning without being a poor design.
recommended_validation: Map accuracy versus range and bus voltage, test deployment from plausible starting poses, and practice the manual-aim fallback. Do not interpret the caption’s repeated “8-inch tube” wording as a verified drum diameter.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Roman I and Roman II solve different feed problems
construction: Roman I uses a rotating floor/center drum and turret; first-party replies describe a roughly 20.75-inch outer drum and 6-inch center, with no fuel compression. Roman II replaces that path with a full-width roller floor and drum shooter. Its floor pivots about an intake dead shaft for electronics access; long four-bar arms fold under impact. The interview contrasts roughly 8 BPS before the rebuild with a reported 23 afterward.
team_stated_reason: The team ties the rebuild to throughput limitations, the net to substantially greater retained inventory, and compact/flexible intake members to avoiding repeated bending. The release specifically credits 5687’s advice with setting Roman II in motion.
engineering_analysis: The strategic change is not simply a faster wheel. Storage, feed width, shooting heading, electrical packaging and intake structure changed together. A comparison should include time spent aiming and avoiding defense, not only an unloaded discharge rate. The original no-compression spindexer and later low-compression drum entry must not be merged into an imaginary hybrid. Service access is especially useful after a rebuild because new routing and wiring require frequent inspection.
recommended_validation: Compare complete-cycle output, residual inventory and defended aiming cost for both versions. Verify rate test conditions, and inspect shaft alignment after lifting the floor for service.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Capstan deployment and belt-floor lanes are dated fixes, not universal upgrades
construction: First-party replies describe 2-inch upper rollers, a 1.25-inch lower roller and about half an inch of compression. The robot changed from roller floor to belt floor between URI and UVM, and from rack deployment to a rope capstan after tooth damage. A 6-inch, 1/8-inch-wall aluminum drum was urethane-coated, machined and balanced; its reported inertia is a little over 80 lb·in².
team_stated_reason: The team says lower collector compression reduced motor bogging. It reports lower current and faster feeding after the belt-floor change; belt spacing created lanes and reduced fuel spinning in place. Rope deployment addressed rack tooth failures, with rope tension becoming the continuing adjustment.
engineering_analysis: This is a useful counterexample to choosing a floor from appearance alone. Belt spacing can organize deformable fuel and remove an unproductive rotating contact state, but that result depends on piece size, belt spacing, load and friction. A capstan cannot skip discrete gear teeth, yet it can slip, stretch, lose tension or suffer anchor damage. The team’s prior capstan experience also changes development risk: the decision was supported by an existing implementation history rather than an untested mechanism adopted casually midseason.
recommended_validation: Test lane stability, residual fuel, electrical demand and rope tension after repeated impacts. Preserve the report that auto shot timers shortened by over half a second without inventing exact before/after BPS.
limitations: Selected first-party replies 14, 16, 21, 23, 38, 40 and 42 in topic 515683, plus code-release topic 524737. This is a discussion/code-release review, not a reviewed technical binder.

title: Small turret throughput cannot be inferred from exterior geometry
construction: First-party replies describe separate X44s for indexer and spindexer, a spinning floor/cone with no deliberate wall compression, and multiple feeder-wheel and ratio trials. The third intake version adds a kicker and movable secondary kicker. The shooter lacks an upper roller; its moving-shot solution combines tuned lookup data and a physics calculation that compensates for spin.
team_stated_reason: The team says the movable kicker resolves earlier collector difficulty and clarifies that the feeder delivers fuel without spin. It does not provide a definitive causal explanation for all of the achieved spindexer throughput. The added flood light helps close-range tag reliability rather than substantially increasing long-range detection.
engineering_analysis: The absence of a counter-roller makes spin an explicit aiming input rather than something to assume away. A compact turret may leave more free hopper area, but the detailed explanation of dead zones and geometry offered by another commenter is expressly an outsider’s hypothesis. Keep that hypothesis separate from the team’s replies. Successful self-unjamming also does not mean jams never occur; the source explicitly acknowledges occasional jams.
recommended_validation: Measure entrance spin and moving-shot error across turret angles, record jam/recovery frequency and time, and inspect exact CAD before copying clearances or interpreting an image-based diameter estimate.
limitations: Selected first-party replies 26, 30, 33, 35 and 47 in topic 515383. Reply 44 is outside analysis, not team intent or a CAD inspection.

title: Floor supply changes the mechanism without replacing the scoring arm
construction: A floor collector was added after Northern Lights while the elevator/arm architecture remained. The retained account identifies roughly 16 pounds of added collector mass, offset by lighter carriage/effector parts. Internal rollers retain coral while the mechanism holds it inverted during algae acquisition. Coral and algae contact regions are offset by about six inches.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly identifies difficult station alignment under defense and successful floor pickups on 1778/2046 as motivations. The offset is described as allowing algae removal and coral placement in one fluid transition.
engineering_analysis: A floor collector should be evaluated as a new cycle source, not an isolated pickup demo. The existing arm must keep coral controlled through the algae motion, and mass must be recovered elsewhere without creating excessive compliance. The six-inch separation is an interface dimension for that combined motion; it is not a universal clearance between any two manipulators.
recommended_validation: Compare defended station cycles with complete floor-to-score cycles, including failed pickups and inverted retention. Check whether the mass-saving parts preserve L4 accuracy and fatigue life.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Self-deploying acquisition still requires indexed possession
construction: A compliant four-bar floor collector feeds a funnel and rotating effector on a two-stage continuous elevator. The retained interview describes reverse roller action deploying the collector. One collector sensor and three arm sensors manage entry, indexing and retention; camera-based acquisition chooses a robot pose relative to the pickup.
team_stated_reason: The team connects floor pickup to shorter coral cycles and describes automatic reef-facing behavior as a way to streamline the driver’s next scoring action. It sought both task-related and climb ranking points.
engineering_analysis: Passive or roller-driven deployment reduces a dedicated actuator but makes friction, game-piece contact and the initial mechanism state part of the deployment logic. Multiple sensors provide intermediate possession states instead of equating “something entered” with “ready to score.” A combined coral/algae mechanism must also preserve the retained object through rotation, not just when stationary.
recommended_validation: Test partial handoffs, skewed coral, deployment without a piece, and failures of each sensor. Verify motor identifiers in CAD/code because automatic captions corrupt model names.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Funnel closure and adaptive grip are separate control problems
construction: A retroreflective beam across the station funnel detects entry and triggers closure before coral rolls to the end effector. An extending roller acquires ground algae. The retained scoring assembly uses an elevator and arm; the climb deploys with a gas shock and captures the cage while the robot advances.
team_stated_reason: The interview describes varying algae-holding voltage using current-related feedback, with more effort when the piece is farther out and less after it is seated. Exact thresholds are not supplied.
engineering_analysis: An entry beam establishes interruption, not orientation or secure final possession. The handoff therefore needs additional state and a recovery path. Adaptive grip can reduce unnecessary loading after capture, but current also changes with friction, compression and voltage; it cannot be treated as a direct position measurement without calibration. The gas-shock climb similarly depends on a defined hard stop and a controlled chassis approach.
recommended_validation: Induce partial entry and bounced coral, measure algae retention at different compression and current, and verify cage capture over realistic lateral offsets.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A telescoping arm avoids a handoff but moves a large work envelope
construction: The interview describes four shoulder motors with a stated 111:1 reduction, a chain-driven dead-axis pivot, and a two-motor telescoping arm. Its wide collector uses front/back roller groups and aluminum centering guides to acquire differently oriented coral; rigid guide plates reflect coral’s low compressibility. The retained record describes extending stage length for L4/net reach.
team_stated_reason: The team links the multi-motor shoulder to power demand. Its acquisition geometry is intended to bring floor coral into the same mechanism that scores it, avoiding a separate transfer.
engineering_analysis: Eliminating a handoff trades transfer risk for arm inertia, sweep clearance and control burden. Extension changes both shoulder torque and the position of the robot’s loaded center of mass. A floor hard stop can define a repeatable pickup plane, but should not be confused with clearance throughout the rest of the motion. Thin coral tolerates less forced compression than foam fuel, so roller selection must be paired with a controlled guide gap.
recommended_validation: Map shoulder current and deflection through extension, test pickup against a wall, and verify coral control during acceleration and sudden chassis braking.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Precision depends on stiffness, backlash and feeding order
construction: A single-stage elevator is driven by chains on both sides to reduce twist; the arm/wrist and shimmed transmissions aim to minimize backlash. The large corrugated-plastic station funnel damps entry. Independently stopped feed rollers can hold coral while the gripper handles algae, and a compact climber fits beneath the funnel.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly treats accuracy as a mechanical and software requirement, identifies dual-sided elevator drive with resisting twist, and explains pausing coral feed during algae possession.
engineering_analysis: A vision system can command the correct pose yet miss a branch if the scoring frame deflects or the transmission reverses through backlash. Hybrid cycles add a scheduling constraint: the incoming coral must not collide with a manipulator that is still gripping algae. The funnel and climber also compete for the same physical space, so a copied climber cannot be assumed to fit behind another team’s station system.
recommended_validation: Measure effector displacement under lateral load and direction reversal; test queued coral while holding algae. Compare repeatability after repeated elevator cycles and drivetrain impacts.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A dedicated low-task arm adds work without monopolizing the elevator
construction: The station funnel uses powered surfaces and an IR entry sensor. The separate Froggy mechanism acquires coral/algae from the floor and scores L1/processor; its source gives a 48:1 X60 pivot and 2:1 X60 roller drive. A linked shaft/chain keeps the side plates synchronized, while added angle reinforcement stiffens their weak direction.
team_stated_reason: The team describes reinforcement after structural analysis and a software interlock that delays retracting Froggy until the chassis backs away from the reef. The main arm’s motor placement is also used for counterbalance.
engineering_analysis: Low-level work can justify a dedicated mechanism when it shortens cycles and releases the primary scorer for another role. That benefit is conditional on interference: two mechanisms must be able to store, acquire and move without colliding. A geometric safety interlock should therefore be part of the architecture reference. “Button released” is not sufficient evidence that an external mechanism can retract safely.
recommended_validation: Test concurrent main-arm/Froggy poses, compare complete L1/algae cycles, and verify retreat detection before retraction under localization error.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Wide pickup, light elevator and faster cage capture solve different delays
construction: A wide four-bar collector feeds the lightweight coral/algae effector on a string-driven continuous elevator. The interview describes thicker carbon after a week-five collector member bent and cracked; the caption does not safely establish the thickness. Later cage guides and capture wheels replace a slower alignment approach.
team_stated_reason: The team links width to driver tolerance, elevator construction to speed/weight/CG, and the revised cage capture to reducing an approximately twenty-second climb process toward roughly ten seconds.
engineering_analysis: The motorized scoring cycle is only one part of match throughput. Wide acquisition can reduce driver correction, while a faster endgame can recover entire scoring cycles. Those gains can justify mass in guides or reinforcement even when they increase subsystem weight. The original and revised climb should not be averaged into one time, and the gain should not be applied to a team whose approach geometry differs.
recommended_validation: Measure failed-pickup rate, full extension deflection and complete cage-approach-to-secured time. Repeat impact tests on the reinforced collector instead of assuming more carbon fixes every load direction.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Differential arm/elevator motion keeps motors low but couples control
construction: The source describes an efficient floor collector, V-shaped powered centering path and a differential elevator/arm transmission. Equal coordinated belt motion translates the carriage; differential motion changes arm angle while the motors stay low. The retained technical record also describes a custom-sealed suction effector and piston/scotch-yoke vacuum source.
team_stated_reason: The team’s explicit objective is short, fast coral cycles and resistance to defense without excessive sacrifice of algae capability. Keeping arm/elevator drive motors at the base serves low moving mass.
engineering_analysis: A differential does not eliminate shoulder or elevator effort; it redistributes that demand across shared actuators. Motion limits, current and saturation must be considered in joint space and motor space. The vacuum end effector can reduce exposed gripping hardware, but seal geometry and surface condition become critical. A short-cycle strategy also needs coordinated human-player supply and a path that avoids interference with partners.
recommended_validation: Test simultaneous lift/rotation near motor limits, vacuum retention on damaged or wet pieces, and recovery after a partially seated coral. Preserve emergency climb acceleration as a high-load exception, not the normal durability baseline.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Cable control and a later algae arm are essential version details
construction: The robot retains an elevator-based station-fed scorer and later adds a compact curved-rack algae intake. A constant-force spring pulls the elevator cable carrier inward after it repeatedly broke, flopped outward or entered the funnel. The climber uses the funnel’s rear region and was revised to grab one cage bar.
team_stated_reason: The team describes the algae arm as lightweight and quick to deploy, and identifies the spring as the response to cable-carrier failures. The updated climb seeks easier capture rather than a larger nominal grasp.
engineering_analysis: A cable carrier is a moving structural interface, not an afterthought in the electrical system. Its force, bend radius and free envelope affect elevator current and what can enter the station funnel. An added algae collector also changes the safe pose space of an already working scorer. The architecture should retain the dated add-on history rather than imply the final robot existed at the first event.
recommended_validation: Run full-stroke cable fatigue tests and check the spring at maximum extension. Test coral loading with the algae mechanism deployed and verify cage capture under angular misalignment.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Wrist freedom creates L1 value and a collision-planning obligation
construction: The team explicitly credits 4414’s 2023 continuous elevator. Its carriage combines a pivot, wrist and compliant coral/algae end effector; range sensors and a transverse wheel actively center coral. The software models tested safe poses and allows only transitions connected in a graph.
team_stated_reason: The interview ties the wrist to effective L1 cycles and the pivot to serving both ground and station acquisition. The restricted transition graph is intended to prevent destructive arm/elevator interactions and overshoot.
engineering_analysis: The wrist should not be justified only by branch reach. It also changes how coral can be presented to the trough, so its value can rise in a low-task alliance role. The price is a larger configuration space: correct endpoint poses do not prove that the path between them is safe. A tested edge graph is a concrete way to carry mechanical clearance assumptions into software.
recommended_validation: Test every allowed transition under lag, sensor error and simultaneous chassis motion. Measure L1 throughput as well as L4 reach, and verify active centering before the final placement motion.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Game simulation preceded the ground-intake commitment
construction: A narrow initial ground concept became a wide collector, feeding an internally belted elevator and arm that can score toward either side. The team reports offseason experience with similar mechanisms. Each software state specifies the collector, elevator, arm and roller setpoints together, with explicit transition conditions.
team_stated_reason: The team describes running match simulations on day two after kickoff to test the significance of unprotected station defense. It connects the floor collector to that strategic result and the monolithic state structure to predictable safe motion.
engineering_analysis: This is a process reference as much as a hardware reference. The team tested a game constraint before committing to a cycle architecture, then used known mechanism families to reduce development risk. Wide acquisition helps only when the handoff can keep up and the arm can safely retract past both field and robot structure. A multi-subsystem state should retain possession information so a timing variation does not silently drop coral.
recommended_validation: Repeat the strategic simulation with plausible opposing and partner robots. Test interrupted transfers and safe recovery from each intermediate state, rather than validating only the nominal score sequence.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Floor orientation and a moving scorer share the alignment workload
construction: The collector uses one motor, a passive guide wall and wheel/roller contact to orient floor coral without a separate vertical-roller stage. A chain-driven lateral slide on Igus guides corrects scorer position. A cascade elevator and custom drivetrain complete the retained architecture.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly connects floor pickup to human players rolling coral near the reef. Its custom-module discussion emphasizes traction and useful gearing rather than adopting an unmodified commercial package.
engineering_analysis: A passive orienter exchanges actuator count for sensitivity to incoming pose, wall friction and driving direction. A lateral scorer can remove some last-meter chassis correction, but it must be stiff enough that the camera’s intended offset corresponds to the actual end-effector position. Ground-source supply and local correction should therefore be assessed as one cycle, including the human player’s delivery error.
recommended_validation: Sample many coral approach orientations and supply distances. Measure lateral-slide backlash/deflection under acceleration, and compare whole-cycle time against a fixed scorer with chassis-only alignment.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A serializer rebuild must eliminate stable wrong orientations
construction: Before Worlds, passive polycarbonate funneling and one lower belt were replaced by molded powered flaps that contact awkward coral orientations. The retained ladder-style placement mechanism also received a cam after early L4 tipping/alignment difficulties. The interview separately describes a ratcheting climb that can retain partial progress after disable.
team_stated_reason: The serializer change is explicitly tied to coral settling into specific trapped orientations. Retaining a climb after power-off is described as an important requirement, not an incidental effect of gearing.
engineering_analysis: A funnel that succeeds in the common orientation can still create a stable mechanical equilibrium in an uncommon one. Powered flaps need to disturb that equilibrium without ejecting or crushing the piece. Likewise, an L4 scorer should be judged by placement stability and alignment delay, not only reaching the nominal height. These are distinct revisions and should not be attributed to one unchanging opening-week robot.
recommended_validation: Deliberately place coral in every previously trapped pose, measure recovery time, and test L4 placement after abrupt chassis stops. Verify retention with the actual disabled climb configuration.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A sideways elevator makes pass-through feasible with different interference
construction: The fourth arm/grabber iteration works beside a sideways-oriented elevator. The robot handles coral levels and algae with the same arm assembly. The interview also describes placing the battery to counter the elevator’s mass and moving the scoring arm clear during climbing.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly says it wanted pass-through behavior but did not consider passing through the elevator suitable for its resources. It identifies low center of gravity as a reason for the alternate arrangement.
engineering_analysis: Pass-through is a functional requirement, not a mandate to send the piece through an elevator opening. An offset mechanism can provide the desired acquisition/scoring directions while changing lateral load, frame torsion and the safe sweep envelope. Counterweight placement may improve static balance but should be checked throughout arm travel and with each game piece.
recommended_validation: Measure lateral deflection and tip margin in the highest off-center pose; test all arm-to-climber transitions. Do not infer an undisclosed collector construction from the functional pass-through description.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Station retention, orientation recovery and fast lift must work together
construction: A post-Niagara ramp/retention change reduces coral bounce-out and permits longer-distance station delivery. Two sensors support orientation detection and unjamming, while the ramp can queue coral during algae possession. The internally belted three-stage elevator has two low motors and tie-rod stiffening; the team reports slightly over half a second to full extension.
team_stated_reason: The source ties the ramp revision directly to entry bounce and the tie rods to rigidity. The retained record describes using an upper roller to redirect coral for L1 as well as higher-level scoring.
engineering_analysis: A fast unloaded lift is valuable only if the queued piece remains controlled and the effector settles accurately. Keeping the next coral on the ramp while holding algae can remove travel from the next cycle, but requires distinct possession states and a deliberate handoff. The reported lift time should remain a mechanism claim rather than a full-cycle time.
recommended_validation: Measure loaded settle time, queued-piece retention during lift motion, and unjamming success for sideways coral. Check cable retention over repeated rapid extensions.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: The rebuild’s full-width intake changes the robot’s supply model
construction: The interview explicitly identifies this as the second robot and says the original lacked the rebuild’s full-width ground collector. Hollow rollers, compliant star wheels and a floating front feed a polycarbonate funnel and sensor-guided handoff. A continuous internally belted elevator and carbon-tube arm carry a shared pinch claw for coral/algae.
team_stated_reason: The team links hollow rollers to weight reduction and identifies the wide ground collector as a major rebuild objective. It reports testing the star-wheel contact choice rather than presenting it as an arbitrary styling decision.
engineering_analysis: The historical lineage should be specific: the team mentions 254’s 2022 hollow-roller construction, while the 2025 task requires orienting rigid coral rather than simply transporting foam cargo. Copying fabrication technique is different from copying an entire intake path. A shared pinch claw can reduce moving mechanisms but its force and retained orientation must remain acceptable for two very different pieces.
recommended_validation: Test pickup orientation tolerance, failed handoff recovery, and claw retention through rapid arm motion. Keep the original and rebuild capabilities separate in recommendations and comparisons.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Protected power and adjustable rigging support a ground-source cycle
construction: The two-stage floor intake keeps its motor inside the chassis, then uses a belt and centering wheel to orient coral. A fixture/beam-break locates the handoff. The continuous elevator has two motors and wrench-adjustable ratchet tensioners for its ropes; a rack positions the shared gripper.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly connects internal motor placement to preventing collision damage and the ratchet arrangement to maintaining rope tension. The interview also demonstrates vision-based coral acquisition.
engineering_analysis: A protected motor still transmits impact through shafts and belts, so the whole load path needs inspection. Adjustable rigging is useful when it makes a repeatable service procedure possible; excessive or unequal tension can add friction and rack a carriage. Vision-directed pickup should be evaluated with the mechanical centering tolerance rather than as an independent AI success.
recommended_validation: Document a reproducible rope-tension procedure, check left/right travel under load, and test handoff after impacts. Measure acquisition success with occlusion and adjacent pieces.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A shorter telescoping arm preserves direct note handling
construction: The arm retains an A-frame/shoulder architecture and reduces the telescope to one moving stage. A guided arm-end collector sends notes directly into the top/bottom-wheel launcher; extension is used for amp and trap. Multiple pose cameras and a note-detection camera support acquisition and scoring.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly says a third stage was unnecessary for the required reach. It identifies avoiding an amp handoff as a reason for consistent amp operation.
engineering_analysis: Reducing extension stages can remove mass, cable length, backlash and maintenance points while retaining the needed task envelope. The comparison must use actual amp/trap geometry and the stage clearance rules, not maximum theoretical arm reach. Direct note handling avoids transfer errors but carries the launcher’s mass and flexible note through the arm’s motion.
recommended_validation: Verify reachable poses and structural deflection at the actual amp/trap approach. Test note retention during fast shoulder motion and clearance under the stage without relying on perfect driver positioning.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Controlled centering preserves deliberately asymmetric shooting contact
construction: A wide compliant/dead-axis intake and guides center the note before an asymmetric launcher contact sequence. The same scoring assembly handles amp delivery and rises for trap work. Beam-break acquisition feedback retracts the collector and rumbles the driver controller.
team_stated_reason: The team identifies driver tolerance, source pickup speed and long-range scoring that reduces driving as priorities. The source reports about a second of cycle improvement from acquisition feedback/retraction behavior; that is a team estimate, not an isolated controlled trial.
engineering_analysis: Ring deformation and lateral offset can change which launcher contact happens first. Centering is therefore part of generating the intended spin, not merely getting the note somewhere inside the robot. The driver-feedback example also shows how a small state signal can reduce wasted acquisition motion without changing motor power.
recommended_validation: Vary lateral entry, note wear and intake speed; measure spin, trajectory spread and complete cycle time. Separate the effect of a wider pickup from the effect of better feedback.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A low pivot and controlled note tunnel protect shot repeatability
construction: A full-width under-bumper collector uses independently driven lateral funneling into a protected ramp/tunnel. The retained source record describes a low rear launcher pivot with separate left/right shooting groups and the same assembly serving amp delivery.
team_stated_reason: The interview emphasizes preserving a continuous note journey and designing for high-level strategic options early. It does not establish that every apparent feature was added specifically for one later playoff tactic.
engineering_analysis: A low tunnel can limit note bending and moving mass, but a protective cover also needs to avoid becoming a new trapping surface. Separately powered funneling allows transport behavior to be tuned without forcing the ground pickup to the same speed. The useful reference is a consistent note state at release; a compact exterior alone does not establish that consistency.
recommended_validation: Test note distortion, off-center entry and cover clearances with worn notes. Compare shot variation after aggressive collection and after gentle hand placement to isolate transport effects.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Staging before selecting a scorer preserves tactical optionality
construction: The collector changed from relatively rigid plates to more flexible material after early bending, with replaceable side assemblies. Two beam breaks track staging before the robot chooses the main shooter or elevated amp/trap path. The team describes an early simple robot, a problematic multi-arm beta and the final architecture.
team_stated_reason: The team connects flexible plates to surviving contact and says the intermediate architecture did not work well. Retaining a staged note before selecting its destination is an explicit feature of the final flow.
engineering_analysis: The branch point in a transfer path is a strategic decision. Delaying the destination choice lets the alliance respond to amplification, traffic or a blocked route without reacquiring the piece. The cost is an extra controlled state that must keep the note centered and releasable. Historical version labels should not collapse the failed beta into the final competition mechanism.
recommended_validation: Test repeated stage-and-wait cycles, destination changes after acquisition and jam recovery at the branch. Evaluate repair time for a damaged collector side as well as pickup speed.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A small robot still needs protection against rare disabling note poses
construction: A compact custom-swerve robot feeds its launcher through pivot-concentric transmission elements. The retained launcher uses four horizontal contacts and a rack-based angle mechanism. A note deflector was added before championships after notes lodged beneath the shooter in two losses; the climb controller corrects roll and coordinates trap release with swing.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly contrasts the season’s small/simple objective with the prior year’s complexity. The deflector is a response to two specific disabling events, not a decorative cover.
engineering_analysis: Rare jams can dominate an otherwise excellent scoring architecture because they remove the whole robot’s contribution. Preventing entry to a bad configuration can be more reliable than detecting and reversing it later. Concentric feeding preserves operation across launcher angles, but actual clearances and moving power transmission still need review. Trap timing based on swing is a separate dynamic-control problem, not proof of static shot accuracy.
recommended_validation: Reproduce the reported under-shooter trap pose, test the deflector with damaged notes, and validate swing/roll compensation under asymmetric chain capture.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Two acquisition directions were the alternative to a turret
construction: The robot has front/rear acquisition, an extended leading roller for wall notes, and a pivoted differential-speed launcher. Reversing the staged note redirects it to the amp/trap carriage. Its swerve uses selectable gearing, with a middle setting in the filmed configuration.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly says turret complexity would burden the intake and handoff, so it chose two intakes instead. It reports fast local cleanup as a benefit; the brief amplified-period claim is a team account, not a universal four-note cycle benchmark.
engineering_analysis: Directional independence can be purchased at the collector instead of the launcher. This can reduce turning during pickup while retaining simpler aiming hardware, but adds a second collision face and more transfer states. The correct comparison is total useful scoring under the expected note distribution and defense, including reversal into the amp carriage.
recommended_validation: Compare opposite-direction acquisition cycles with a one-intake baseline, and test handoff after a note enters off-center from either side.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Omni centering and reoriented transfer need defined staging states
construction: Omni wheels and printed wedges center the note while allowing lateral motion. The rotating shooter aligns with the intake to receive it; paired sensors detect travel and possession. The same moving assembly uses gentle roller release for amp/trap rather than a high-speed shot.
team_stated_reason: The team identifies lateral freedom as the reason for the omni contact choice. Sensor feedback reduces the driver’s need to see the note and helps avoid acquiring a second piece.
engineering_analysis: A roller can create useful forward traction while resisting necessary lateral centering. Omni contact addresses that conflict, but the wedges still establish the note’s final alignment. A moving transfer interface adds a temporal constraint: feeding must wait for receiving geometry, then stop at a verified state before reorientation. Gentler release for a confined goal is a separate control mode from speaker firing.
recommended_validation: Test diagonal entries and sensor disagreement; measure capture/transfer tolerances at the rotating interface and retention during the following motion.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Low moving mass and rapid prototyping support a multi-task pivot
construction: A protected under-bumper collector and polycord conveyor feed a central pivoted scoring assembly. Motors sit near the pivot and long belt runs carry power outward. Independent shooting sides provide note spin; the same mechanism serves ground pickup, speaker and amp poses.
team_stated_reason: The source describes selecting objectives at kickoff, prototyping multiple launcher types and using short print/test iterations to resolve problems. Its under-bumper choice emphasizes collision protection.
engineering_analysis: Moving motors toward the pivot can reduce rotational inertia, but long belts introduce compliance, tension and replacement considerations. A shared pivot simplifies the number of mechanisms while making each pose and connecting motion more important. Rapid printed iterations are a development capability that another team must budget for, rather than assume it receives by copying the final CAD.
recommended_validation: Measure belt-related angular lag and shot variation after fast pivot moves. Reproduce the complete pickup-to-score path, and include repair/reprint time in the architecture comparison.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Minimal intake rollers and redundant climb capacity have different justifications
construction: The over-bumper collector uses four rollers after early prototyping. An indexer retains the note and serves amp delivery through a virtual linkage. The top/bottom launcher uses asymmetric wheel contact. Each climber has two motors, and the team describes continuing after one side was removed following a failure.
team_stated_reason: The team ties the reduced collector to sufficient pickup performance with lower mass, and the unusual climb power to single-side operation and imperfect chain alignment. Asymmetric contact is reported to improve spin/stability and range.
engineering_analysis: Simplicity should be evaluated per task rather than imposed uniformly. Removing an unnecessary roller can improve collector dynamics, while adding climb reserve can preserve a match outcome after damage. Those are compatible engineering decisions. Single-side climbing also changes structural loads and roll, so redundancy is only real if the frame and scoring mechanisms tolerate the alternate load case.
recommended_validation: Test the minimum collector with worn notes and wall contact. Validate disabled-side climb loading and harmony clearance, rather than extrapolating from two-side nominal lifts.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A central selector and elevator trade travel for transfer complexity
construction: A nearly full-width intake centers notes with wedges. The central carriage can direct a note to the rear pivoting launcher or retain it for the three-stage internally belted amp/trap elevator. Separate launcher speeds create spin; printed supports maintain belt tension.
team_stated_reason: The source connects the launcher speed difference to stable flight and describes selecting the destination in the middle of the robot. The retained source does not establish a numerical optimum for the offset frame geometry.
engineering_analysis: Central selection preserves task choice but creates a bidirectional handoff that must be indexed consistently. An elevator can place accurately at close targets while a rear launcher serves range; the benefit must exceed transfer delay, extra mass and the chance of a note straddling two mechanisms. Frame offsets also require checking the support polygon at elevated scoring poses.
recommended_validation: Test direction reversals with a partially transferred note, measure elevator settle and belt tension drift, and verify the homing procedure after mechanical service.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Compliant bumper entry and a supported pivot solve separate uncertainties
construction: Spring-loaded under-bumper collector segments compress notes through a limited opening, with an additional over-bumper collector. A sensor-tracked conveyor stages the note. The launcher angle is driven on both sides, and the source describes protecting the separate position sensor/transmission from damage.
team_stated_reason: The team connects the two-sided pivot drive to reducing wobble and describes launcher changes made to gain useful shooting distance. The independent collector segments are intended to acquire at a wall as well as in open space.
engineering_analysis: Compliant entry can increase tolerance while making the note’s shape and arrival speed variable. The downstream stage must restore a repeatable state before release. A symmetric pivot support helps angular repeatability, but the stiffness of the frame and belt/chain tension still determine the actual output angle.
recommended_validation: Measure entry success at bumper contact, note deformation after transport, and left/right pivot deflection under acceleration. Verify stage sensing before comparing range.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Any-heading note loading is the prerequisite for a useful turret
construction: Under-bumper acquisition feeds four vertical rollers that move the note around the turret’s receiving cage. A light amp guide directs an upward release. The source describes a late, simple worm-drive climb and software superstates that coordinate turret, feeder and launcher rather than binding unrelated commands independently.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly emphasizes feeding at different turret headings. Climb packaging was constrained by its late addition, motivating simplicity and low mass.
engineering_analysis: A turret adds little directional independence if it must return to one heading to acquire every note. The receiving cage and its contact sequence are therefore as important as aiming range. A superstate helps express the common readiness condition, but needs fault handling when only some mechanisms reach their setpoints. A worm transmission should not be assumed to hold every load without checking its actual efficiency and disabled behavior.
recommended_validation: Measure transfer success versus heading, note wear and acceleration. Test partial readiness, cable limits and power-off climb retention. The viewer-disabled binder remains unreviewed; do not substitute a guessed download.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Pivot-settle delay and belt skipping require dated evidence
construction: The build thread records replacing a slower, note-damaging conveyor with a more direct curved feed, carbon-roller shooter changes, replaceable intake assemblies and pivot stiffening. Later posts describe a friction damper, changing pivot belts, a ratio change from 125:1 to 100:1, and Worlds logs exposing belt skipping when the arm extended.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly ties the direct feed to speed/note preservation, the damper to waiting several seconds for the angle to settle, and the revised ratio to faster rotation. Log comparison between motor and external encoder exposed a mechanical slip rather than merely a software aiming error.
engineering_analysis: This history explains why commanded angle, measured motor angle and true launcher angle are different quantities. Increasing control gains cannot reliably fix a slipping transmission. The fastest pivot also is not the one with the shortest complete aim-to-shot time if it oscillates afterward. The early proposal to climb using the shooter must remain a proposal unless later installation evidence supports it.
recommended_validation: Compare motor and external encoder trajectories under arm extension, measure request-to-exit latency, and inspect intake damage after contact.
limitations: First-party build posts in topic 452466, especially 2, 5, 21, 27 and 32. The previously linked w0AFxJFMOqg video is match/driver audio, not a technical interview; it is rejected as construction evidence here.

title: Contact geometry and fast wheel service both affect available scoring
construction: Front/rear intake paths stage a note on low-friction support and feed a pivoting transfer. The launcher uses four Vortex-driven contact groups after tests with fewer contacts. The interview also discusses rapidly replaceable printed wheel components, reporting swaps in under a minute when a replacement is prepared.
team_stated_reason: The team says earlier arrangements did not provide sufficient contact and that additional roller power/placement emerged through testing. Serviceability was deliberately considered for playoff repair windows.
engineering_analysis: Motor count is the consequence of a contact requirement, not a standalone design target. Each contact must accelerate without deforming the note into a less repeatable state. Repair speed affects how much performance survives a tournament: a fast but fragile part may be viable only if replacement stock and access are designed at the same time.
recommended_validation: Compare slip, note deformation and release speed across contact arrangements. Time an actual module replacement with match-ready tools and verify the resulting alignment.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Consistent staging is needed before a multi-pose launcher can be accurate
construction: A roller collector feeds a compliant-wheel launcher that rises on an elevator for amp and trap. Three distance sensors establish note position; magnetic switches protect climb travel. Trap execution changes hooks, elevator height and launcher angle in a defined sequence.
team_stated_reason: The source explicitly connects the distance sensors to placing the note consistently and the limit devices to preventing mechanism damage. More exact intake material/ratio details are not established by the selected caption passages.
engineering_analysis: One launcher serving several targets reduces duplicate release hardware but changes gravity, retention and moving mass across poses. A correct angle table assumes a repeatable note position. The climb/trap sequence must also avoid moving the launcher through the chain or frame while partially loaded.
recommended_validation: Test staged-note position spread, sensor disagreement and retention during elevator motion. Validate the complete trap sequence with realistic swing and lateral approach error.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Centering, spin and reverse transfer share one constrained path
construction: Silicone-wrapped collector rollers, Teflon-covered wedges and additional module guides center the note. A two-roller feeder can reverse it into the backpack amp/trap path. Asymmetric black-wheel placement produces spin, while the main scoring pivot uses sector gearing with reinforcement.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly identifies the full-width intake with driver margin and the contact materials with centering. The backpack receives the note through a reversed feed sequence.
engineering_analysis: Forward and reverse transport must both control a flexible ring. A low-friction wedge is useful for centering but may provide little retention while the robot reverses direction or lifts the note. The launcher’s intended asymmetry also depends on repeatable centering. A shared path saves hardware only if direction changes do not create a high jam or alignment burden.
recommended_validation: Test reversed handoffs after aggressive pickup, measure note pose before each route, and verify chain clearance through the climb/backpack sequence.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: The rebuild traded turret freedom for structure and long-range consistency
construction: The source distinguishes the original turret from a rebuilt fixed-heading launcher. The rebuild changes drive tubes to 3×1, belly-pan thickness to 3/16 inch and base dimensions to 26×27.5 inches. Protected dead-axis feed and four-motor differential-speed shooting serve long range; reverse feeding sends a note to the amp elevator.
team_stated_reason: The team reports structural problems affecting under-bumper acquisition and insufficient original turret power for its preferred long shot. It decided the turret’s advantages did not outweigh its costs for the intended robot functions.
engineering_analysis: This is a strategic architecture rejection with concrete technical causes. A turret is not automatically superior when its packaging reduces stiffness, collection quality or release capability. The fixed-heading replacement must still pay chassis-aiming time and defended heading constraints, so the reason applies to the team’s specific route/shot strategy rather than every Crescendo robot.
recommended_validation: Compare full acquisition-to-release time and range under defense, inspect frame deflection, and test reversed amp transfer after long shots. Preserve original/rebuild boundaries in any inspiration sentence.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Different contact stiffness enables amp delivery without a pivot
construction: The under-bumper collector and guides feed two independently driven launcher rollers. The interview describes a lower-durometer lower contact relative to the upper contact, combined with speed control, to curve the amp delivery without moving the whole launcher. A deflector protects the climber from dropped notes.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly chose the contact/speed arrangement to perform both speaker and amp tasks without a pivot, with robustness as a stated benefit. The climber guard responds to the possibility of a falling note disabling it.
engineering_analysis: Eliminating an angle actuator shifts trajectory control into contact deformation, spin and launch speed. That reduces joints and moving wiring, but may increase sensitivity to note wear, temperature and compression. The guard illustrates that a rare dropped piece can create a structural failure state even when the main transport path works.
recommended_validation: Map amp accuracy with used notes, varying voltage and repeated shooting. Test the dropped-note guard from several directions and verify that it does not obstruct normal climbing.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Routing the note and routing the chain are both architecture interfaces
construction: A full-width collector uses leading rollers, wedges and slippery passive centering surfaces. The indexer selects the main shooter or rack-driven amp/trap backpack. Double-sided belts package opposite roller directions. Climb-side fangs guide the chain over areas where it could catch the shooter/backpack; four pose cameras use deliberately different views/lenses.
