team_stated_reason: The source explicitly connects the fangs to avoiding chain entrapment and the camera arrangement to useful tag visibility on approach to scoring locations. It treats camera placement as a deliberate strategy choice rather than simply adding identical cameras.
engineering_analysis: A compact scorer and climber can each work separately but fail when a flexible chain sweeps through their shared space. Passive routing surfaces are therefore a mechanism interface, not cosmetic guards. Similarly, extra cameras help only when their sight lines and uncertainty provide information the existing views lack.
recommended_validation: Test chain capture with lateral error and robot roll, inspect every backpack handoff, and measure pose availability along the intended routes rather than only at a parked test position.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A broad angle range needs controlled note position and a fallback pose estimate
construction: Six collector rollers, gripping wrap and reinforced polycarbonate feed a bent note path. Sensors distinguish staging and the amp/shooter route. The interview reports an adjustable launch range approximately 17–65 degrees with automatic speed/angle selection; pose estimation continues through brief vision loss.

engineering_analysis: A numerical angle range is a mechanical envelope, not a guarantee that every field position is accurate. Flexible notes arrive with different deformation and velocity, while pose confidence may degrade during occlusion. The appropriate architecture includes a readiness condition and safe fallback, not just an interpolation table.
recommended_validation: Measure staged pose, accuracy versus range/angle, and performance after controlled vision dropout. Verify actual angular limits in code or CAD before reusing the caption numbers.

title: Symmetric acquisition and sufficient release clearance are different requirements
construction: A vertically symmetric gripper acquires cubes and upright/tipped cones from either robot face. A continuous lift uses synchronized sides, guides and adjustable structural stays. The interview reports redesigning the claw to open farther because cubes remained trapped after the release command.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly ties gripper symmetry to the arm working on both sides. The larger opening responds to failed cube release rather than poor initial acquisition.
engineering_analysis: A mechanism that holds both pieces well can still release one poorly. Compliant foam and tapered cones create different contact/retention conditions, so acquisition success is not a substitute for a release test. Through-robot arm travel also makes lift parallelism and cable clearance part of both scoring directions.
recommended_validation: Measure release delay and remaining contact for worn cubes, test cone orientation extremes, and check lift binding after frame contact.

title: Split rack collectors preserve a central arm corridor
construction: Two cantilevered rack-and-pinion collector halves leave space for a telescoping arm, synchronized by a cross-shaft with service couplers. The shoulder transmission is nested below the arm; a compact wrist and roller claw complete direct scoring.
team_stated_reason: The team identifies robust, controllable deployment and avoiding pneumatics as reasons for the rack choice. Shoulder placement is tied to maximizing useful stowed arm length.
engineering_analysis: The center gap is not wasted intake width: it is clearance purchased for another mechanism. Synchronization must keep both collector halves from racking while still permitting fast replacement. As the arm extends, gravity torque rises with lever arm, so tuning only the retracted shoulder does not establish controllability at high reach.
recommended_validation: Test one-sided collector impacts, service-coupler realignment and shoulder tracking at maximum extension with each game piece.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A borrowed belt gripper needs its operating clearance, not just its layout
construction: The polyurethane-belt gripper credits WildStang’s published work. Stand-offs keep running belts away from the carpet. A continuously rigged, internally belted elevator leaves an open arm passage; an auxiliary cube collector is discussed as a later low/link opportunity.
team_stated_reason: The team cites grip on cones, carpet protection and keeping elevator gearing/mass low. The auxiliary collector must remain a proposal unless its later fielded configuration is established.
engineering_analysis: Copying the contact belt without its stand-offs can create both carpet damage and an unintended ground reaction on the arm. A low-mounted drive reduces moving mass, while an open passage permits acquisition on the opposite side. The strategic value of an added cube collector depends on finishing links quickly, not simply acquiring another mechanism.
recommended_validation: Test floor clearance under chassis pitch, compare both piece types, and measure complete low-node cycles before adding the proposed subsystem.

title: Commercial structure and deletion of an unnecessary roller reduce development work
construction: The robot adapts a WCP GreyT elevator with two Falcons and a narrower configuration. The gripper evolves from side-grabbing concepts toward Everybot-style upper cone/lower cube contacts; an extra powered roller is removed after tests showed it was unnecessary.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly identifies commercial elevator parts as compatible with its manufacturing resources and describes the third roller as large and awkward without sufficient benefit. Swerve adoption was preceded by offseason work.
engineering_analysis: The useful reference is a tested simplification, not a claim that commercial hardware requires no engineering. Narrowing a standard structure changes bearing loads, stiffness and packaging. Removing a contact is justified when the remaining contacts retain acquisition and release tolerance across real piece conditions.
recommended_validation: Test the narrowed elevator for racking, validate pickup after collector deletion with worn pieces, and include offseason drive-training time in any comparison.

title: Remote wrist actuation and practiced direct pickup avoid a second collector
construction: A small square chassis carries a shoulder/elbow/wrist arm with low-mounted transmissions and a remote aircraft-cable wrist drive. Fixed gripper spacing handles both pieces. A separate Rapid React-style collector was prototyped but not adopted; arm motion uses waypoint/path-following ideas related to the drivetrain tools.
team_stated_reason: The team connects chassis size to maneuverability and says the added collector was unnecessary after substantial practice with the existing gripper, with integration and retraining costs outweighing expected benefit.
engineering_analysis: A theoretical faster acquisition mechanism can be a worse late-season choice if it consumes development and driver time without improving full-cycle reliability. Remote cable drive reduces distal motor mass but makes tension, stretch and backlash important. Safe endpoint waypoints also do not certify the swept volume between them.
recommended_validation: Measure wrist hysteresis, arm clearance throughout each path, and direct-pickup performance under realistic misalignment before reviving the rejected collector.

title: A compliant collector must hand off at the actual revised arm geometry
construction: A low-pivot collector uses mecanum/omni contact to center a tipped cone, then rotates it toward a narrow gripper. The extending scoring arm keeps its transmission low and measures actual arm angle beyond gearbox backlash. Shoulder-style bearing support helps retain bearings in flexible plates.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly credits Grasshoppers inspiration, seeks fast/light centering and explains the low collector pivot as letting impacts lift the mechanism rather than break it. Handoff angle changes must follow hardware revisions.
engineering_analysis: A wide pickup can improve acquisition while increasing the range of states presented to a narrow receiver. Compliance helps survive contact but must not erase the repeatable pose needed for transfer. Measuring the joint after transmission backlash improves observability; it does not mechanically remove the backlash.
recommended_validation: Test handoff after collector impacts, compare actual and motor-side angle under reversals, and verify bearing retention after repeated plate flex.

title: Simple continuous rigging still requires deliberate line management
construction: An Everybot-derived wide roller gripper handles cones and cubes from a common floor pose. A remote chain drives the wrist while keeping its gearbox low. The continuous elevator uses line guides/guards instead of relying solely on a grooved spool; the interview reports many collector iterations.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly links continuous rigging to fewer strings/failure opportunities and identifies the guards as a way to maintain self-spooling without sacrificing the intended structure.
engineering_analysis: A common pickup pose reduces driver and software branching, but different pieces still need different contact/retention behavior. Low motors reduce moving mass while remote transmission adds slack and tension considerations. “Fewer strings” is a mechanism-specific simplification, not proof that rigging is insensitive to line stacking or abrasion.
recommended_validation: Run repeated full-travel cycles with realistic line tension, test both pieces at the edges of the acquisition zone, and inspect remote-wrist backlash after impact.

title: Direct acquisition keeps the subsystem count low but makes reach geometry decisive
construction: A swerve chassis carries an arm with an extending elevator and end roller collector, acquiring directly from the floor and single substation and reaching all grid levels. No independent transfer mechanism is established in the reviewed passage.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly seeks a simple, robust, efficient robot and identifies this as its first competition season using swerve. The caption’s combined module/gearing terminology needs a hardware check before treating it as a part specification.
engineering_analysis: Direct pickup removes a handoff, but reach, wrist attitude and ground clearance must all be solved by the scoring mechanism. A successful demonstration at one field location does not prove access to every node with realistic partner traffic. First-year swerve readiness also consumes tuning and practice capacity that belongs in the design decision.

title: Deployable bash guards protect a collector but can obstruct scoring
construction: An Everybot-style roller gripper and flipping wrist acquire cones from either direction. Deployable side bash guards move with the exposed collector. Lift and wrist motion overlap to reduce delay, while driver modes control guard behavior.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly says preventing damage is preferable to repeatedly replacing the collector. It also notes that guards should not deploy during scoring because they would contact the wall.
engineering_analysis: A protective structure changes the collision envelope it is intended to manage. It can improve floor acquisition under defense while creating a new field-contact risk near the grid. The safe state therefore includes the guards, not only the arm and gripper. Overlapped motions save time only if their intermediate envelopes remain clear.
recommended_validation: Test lateral collector impacts, scoring-wall clearance and interrupted transitions. Measure full pickup-to-release time with the guard interlocks active.

title: Low arm mass and repeatable collect stops support a large reach envelope
construction: A lightweight shoulder/elbow arm with low transmissions carries a three-roller claw. The collect pose bears against a rigid bumper support and stays contained. The team reports an approximately 17-pound arm assembly; module selection also considered ground clearance and packaging.
team_stated_reason: The source explicitly emphasizes reducing mass given the required outward/upward reach and credits Citrus-style claw ideas while making the implementation smaller and lighter. Cube compression is chosen to retain rather than damage the piece.
engineering_analysis: A mechanical collect stop can define acquisition geometry more repeatably than a high-gain servo alone, provided the bumper/support does not move unpredictably. Reducing distal mass improves torque demand and balance, but must preserve stiffness at maximum reach. Ground-clearance decisions also affect charge-station behavior and any intended special climbing approach.
recommended_validation: Measure deflection at full reach, test pickup after bumper displacement, and verify retention across both piece types and abrupt chassis motion.

title: Backlash and compliant handoff tolerance must be separated
construction: A floor beater/roller collector hands pieces to a shoulder/elbow arm and claw. The source describes high shoulder loads and early slop problems. The wider claw accommodates variable lateral arrival and can also acquire at the shelf.
team_stated_reason: The team ties a rigid shoulder transmission to consistent placement and the wide/compliant receiver to successful handoff from a broad collector.
engineering_analysis: Useful compliance at the receiver is different from uncontrolled angular lost motion at the shoulder. One enlarges acquisition tolerance; the other shifts the end-effector position unpredictably at the node. A good transfer should center or otherwise define the retained piece before the arm uses precision scoring poses.
recommended_validation: Measure piece-position spread after handoff separately from arm-position hysteresis. Test both shelf and ground acquisition, including incomplete transfers and reversals.

title: Buffered cube supply and separate reach axes create an alliance tool
construction: A wide overhead cube collector funnels through an internal tunnel to a claw. Separate vertical and horizontal elevator axes plus an articulated arm provide reach. The interview distinguishes normal cone pickup from a slower tipped-cone uprighting maneuver.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly describes designing for high-level play and wanting a differentiated capability. The physical room for multiple pieces is not permission to possess them outside the applicable protected zones.
engineering_analysis: Buffering can decouple human-player delivery from the next placement, but only within the game’s legal possession constraints. Extra reach axes also create collision and maintenance demands. The slower cone fallback is capability, not evidence it is the preferred cycle.
recommended_validation: Test legal buffered operation, tunnel recovery, both-axis settling and cone fallback cycle cost.

title: A narrower claw purchases access to contested low geometry
construction: A narrow gripper handles both pieces, with a wide tilted cascading elevator and wrist. Cross-bracing resists parallelogram deformation; shimmed gearing and a chain wrist reduce play under the collector load.
team_stated_reason: The retained account ties claw width to fitting between hybrid dividers for retrieval/re-scoring. The team says a chain held the wrist load better than its belt trial.
engineering_analysis: Maximum acquisition width is not always optimal. A smaller receiver can access a task a wider collector cannot, provided pickup tolerance remains acceptable. Elevator tilt can improve approach geometry while changing tip margin and wrist loads.
recommended_validation: Measure pickup tolerance, low-node retrieval clearance, wrist hysteresis and full-extension stability.

title: A familiar carbon elevator reduces development uncertainty, not every failure mode
construction: A wide cube collector feeds the upper gripper while cones use direct acquisition. A carbon elevator tilts on a sector mechanism; an escape region avoids trapping a second piece.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly cites prior carbon-elevator experience, limited build time and a desire for reliable fast scoring. Low mass addresses concern about crossing the charge station with a tall structure.

recommended_validation: Test charge-station pitch with the mechanism safely stowed, tilt stiffness and rejection of an unintended extra piece.

title: A compact telescoping package still needs piece-specific poses
construction: A two-stage telescoping arm, shoulder and wrist provide grid reach while stowing low. The source demonstrates distinct floor-cube, tipped-cone, upright-cone and shelf-acquisition poses using dead-axis roller contacts.
team_stated_reason: The stated objectives are speed, compactness, all-level reach and low center of gravity.

title: Separate contact development can outperform one compromised gripper

title: A week-zero prototype must not be treated as the final competition configuration

title: A virtual linkage must preserve useful contact at every task pose
construction: A curved roller gripper directly acquires both pieces on a virtual-four-bar/extension architecture. Linkage/sprocket geometry serves floor, station and scoring positions; holding rollers idle at lower speed in the last useful direction.
team_stated_reason: The team identifies fast cycles and a wide acquisition aperture as priorities, and describes testing drivetrain/contact choices for charge-station traction.
engineering_analysis: A virtual linkage can coordinate joints mechanically, but its coupled path still needs field/robot clearance. Idle roller direction must match possession state or it can eject the wrong piece.
recommended_validation: Test every acquisition/release pose, interrupted transitions and low-speed holding under chassis acceleration.

title: A wide elevator enables a later collector, with a real packaging cost
construction: A belted elevator and chained virtual four-bar place a shared claw. A later cube collector passes through the elevator opening. The source describes a custom second drive motor on each module and a nominal ratio/speed claim.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly says the wide opening made the late cube handoff possible. Additional drive power is a configuration-specific choice, not a requirement for every copied elevator.

title: Passive cone reorientation removes an axis only if the handoff remains tolerant
construction: A two-stage elevator has an overextending carriage and internally routed Dyneema. The rear collector vectors cubes and uses a compliant cone handoff to correct orientation before the scoring gripper receives it.
team_stated_reason: The source links internal line routing to avoiding snags. The retained account describes passive cone reorientation in place of another controlled axis.
engineering_analysis: Moving orientation work into compliance reduces actuator/control count while making friction, piece pose and guide geometry decisive. Internal rigging protects lines but complicates inspection and replacement.
recommended_validation: Test extreme cone approaches, worn pieces and line service access; distinguish smooth demo transfer from statistical handoff reliability.

title: Deliberately omitted floor cones preserve a reliable preferred cycle
construction: A double-jointed arm keeps both joint transmissions low. A wide cube collector uses compliant guides; cones are acquired at the double station rather than through a floor-cone mechanism. Collector material iterations address trapped or damaged cubes.
team_stated_reason: The team chooses arm freedom to permit software iteration and targets rapid pickup-to-setpoint motion. The retained account explicitly omits floor cones in favor of reliable station work.
engineering_analysis: Missing a task can be a deliberate architectural trade. That trade depends on station access under defense and the cost of a failed floor recovery, not a blanket claim that floor cones lack value.

title: Two piece modes coordinate a tilted elevator and motorized wrist
construction: An Everybot-inspired gripper changes wheel orientation and adds retaining netting for cubes. A tilted elevator and wrist acquire and place directly; software coordinates mode-specific heights, wrist angles and roller directions.
team_stated_reason: The source identifies containment and shared piece handling as the gripper’s purpose. Color cues indicate the selected mode; they are not themselves a vision classification result.
engineering_analysis: A shared effector needs different states for different pieces. Confusing selected cone/cube mode with sensed possession can produce the wrong approach or release even if every motor reaches its setpoint.
recommended_validation: Test mode disagreement, partial pickup and retention during tilt/wrist movement.

title: Removing contact points can improve cargo flow
construction: The collector was repeatedly revised to remove dead zones and pinch points. A pneumatic gate separates stored cargo from the launcher, with a kicker and two capacity sensors. The retained source distinguishes main/back-wheel choices and a sequential traversal climb.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly ties collector iteration to reliable acquisition rather than simply higher roller speed.
engineering_analysis: A gate decouples possession from launch readiness. More grip can create an unwanted stable pinch, so the test must include side-by-side cargo and partial entry, not only single clean pickups.
recommended_validation: Measure jam/recovery frequency and feed latency with worn cargo; test gate timing during wheel recovery.

title: Acceleration, protected acquisition and climb CG were iterated separately
construction: The retained technical account describes a compliant dead-axis intake, isolated kicker, turret and adjustable hood. A coarser hood rack addressed skipping. The interview describes changing drivetrain gearing for acceleration under defense and shifting climb CG by rotating the arm.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly reports insufficient acceleration after States and a one-to-two-second climb improvement from the CG change.
engineering_analysis: Maximum free speed is not defended cycle performance. Climb timing also depends on gravitational motion and hook approach, not merely winch speed. Separate the filmed later configuration from earlier competitions.
recommended_validation: Measure loaded acceleration, hood backlash and repeatable climb completion, preserving the reported timing conditions.

title: Impact-resistant acquisition and reduced spin require coordinated contacts
construction: A wide dead-axis collector feeds a curved S-path and hooded launcher with powered upper contacts to reduce backspin. The interview discusses planned bouncing-cargo improvements and future climb automation, while the filmed climb remains manually sequenced.
team_stated_reason: The source explicitly identifies fast acquisition and impact resistance as collector priorities.

title: Low hardware placement and staged turret feeding share scarce volume
construction: An inverted swerve arrangement moves motors low, while a protected collector and printed guide feed staged cargo to the turret. A limit switch and color sensor support possession/rejection. The climb uses retained hooks and a rotating arm.
team_stated_reason: The team identifies top-side packaging space as a reason for the inverted modules. More exact collector optimization intent remains in the retained source bundle rather than the selected excerpt.

title: A productive scorer may rationally skip the climb in some playoff roles
construction: A compliant four-bar collector and belt centering feed a turret/hood launcher. Capacity indicators and operator rejection coordinate cargo state. The automated climb is contrasted with continuing to shoot.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly says two partners capable of traversal can make continued scoring preferable in playoffs, while qualification bonus needs may require its climb.

title: Break symmetric jams and choose a reliable climb pace
construction: Foam collector contacts replace earlier rubber/mecanum choices; agitation addresses two-cargo jams. The retained account describes staged wrong-color ejection, a powered upper roller added after South Florida and a hooded turret. The team reports a roughly ten-second traversal with faster but less reliable trials.
team_stated_reason: The source explicitly prefers the slightly slower climb because faster operation sometimes behaves unpredictably.

recommended_validation: Measure full-cycle jam rate, rejection interactions and climb success versus timing, not only best-case speed.

title: Independent rejection avoids disturbing the entire transport path
construction: An over-bumper vectored collector narrows into a ball-width throat. The retained technical account describes independently driven compliant contacts, a larger lower roller to remove a dead region and a fixed-heading two-position hood launcher.

title: Sensor latency and passive hood compliance are deliberate constraints

title: An offset path changes both cargo control and partner climb clearance
construction: Separate front/rear elevator belts oppose to retain cargo and run together to feed an offset fixed-heading launcher. Color/IR staging supports rear rejection. A driver alignment flap helps place the robot for a shared hangar climb.

title: Late winglets improve edge acquisition without changing the core scorer
construction: An unequal four-bar with compliant plates receives later deployable winglets/belts to address edge jams. Sensor-tracked slots and an independent ejector select retained versus wrong-color cargo; the hood lineage credits 2910.

title: Moving shots require a state model beyond distance alone
construction: A compliant-link collector feeds horizontal/vertical conveyors and a low-driven turret. The source describes a shot model using distance and chassis velocity components to select hood angle and wheel speed.
team_stated_reason: The retained construction uses linkage compliance for impact survival; the interview explains compensating radial and tangential motion in the aiming solution.

title: Long-lived turret experience does not remove staging and rejection requirements
construction: A floating broad collector and mecanum centering feed two-stage transport with color sensing and rejection recovery. The turret/launcher family has several historical iterations, including earlier-season examples, with controlled backspin in this version.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly describes iteration of a familiar turret family rather than a wholly new 2022 mechanism.
engineering_analysis: Existing know-how can reduce development risk, but the new game’s piece state, rejection legality and contact path still require testing. A rejected ball may disturb the next staged piece, so recovery is part of useful cycle time.
recommended_validation: Test rejection followed immediately by scoring and verify turret range/cable limits with the actual 2022 configuration.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A bounded shooting envelope can be an intentional simplification
construction: The collector moves from early flap/Velcro contacts through rubber to a later griptape tube. Breakaway members protect the core. A fixed-heading, fixed-elevation launcher uses a powered back roller and accepts a bounded shooting region; the climb uses swing to reach traversal.
team_stated_reason: The source explicitly reports early contacts repelling cargo and later material experiments. The retained account treats the limited shooting area as an accepted design constraint.
engineering_analysis: Range is not free capability. A simpler scorer can be effective if its reachable positions, acquisition routes and defended access remain adequate. Offseason material changes must not be back-projected onto Worlds.
recommended_validation: Test access to the preferred scoring area under defense and compare collector materials with consistent cargo and approach speed.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Climb-or-shoot is a partner-dependent allocation decision
construction: A wide collector centers moving cargo and was reinforced after impact damage. A vertical conveyor/color stage feeds a roughly ±175-degree turret with two hood states. The interview reports a roughly ten-to-fifteen-second best climb range.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly says reliable traversal partners can make continued shooting the preferable assignment.
engineering_analysis: The comparison must include travel, capture, retries and available cargo, not only mechanism lift time. This demonstrates marginal task value in 2022 without making any claim that its climb incentive matches 2026.
recommended_validation: Measure scored output during the entire climb interval and validate shared-climb reliability before fixing the alliance’s endgame allocation.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Frame and climb objectives can justify an unusual drivetrain
construction: The source describes an octagonal five-module chassis, asymmetric collector contact for adjacent cargo and a turreted launcher. At the filmed event, alignment for its special climb remains manual; floor-line sensors are planned.
team_stated_reason: The team links frame length to its truss-climb approach and the fifth module to stability while driving.
engineering_analysis: An unusual module count cannot be evaluated independently of the task geometry that produced it. Added contact and mass may help stability while increasing power, scrub and service burden. Planned alignment sensors cannot be credited to the filmed result.
recommended_validation: Measure traction/current, alignment success and shared-climb clearance with the actual event configuration.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Stored launcher energy and explicit hook confirmation reduce different risks
construction: The retained account describes a large flywheel/long contact wrap, powered upper contacts, an adjustable hood and a top-driven path over the battery. Climb control confirms both mid-bar hooks before starting the automatic sequence.
team_stated_reason: The team connects low swerve motor placement to CG and packaging, and explains hook confirmation as preventing a one-hook climb that could break hardware.
engineering_analysis: A fast automated sequence should begin from a verified mechanical state. Similarly, high flywheel energy helps paired shots only if the feed preserves contact and motor power restores speed between volleys.
recommended_validation: Test partial hook capture, full two-ball release and recovery at realistic battery conditions.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Repeated intake iterations must remain attached to the correct shooter snapshot
construction: The team reports several whole-robot iterations. The retained account distinguishes early pneumatic flex-wheel collection from later motorized rollers, sensor-tracked cargo chambers, a wide-range turret and a high-mounted targeting camera.
team_stated_reason: The interview emphasizes rapid fabrication/iteration and material testing. More exact performance attribution requires the dated release/configuration, not the number of iterations alone.
engineering_analysis: A camera mounted to preserve near-goal visibility changes the available aiming envelope. Color/rejection and staged possession must still coordinate with turret direction. Do not combine every photographed intake into one version.
recommended_validation: Validate close-range sight lines, rejection trajectory and intake/feed readiness after a mechanism swap.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Collapsible acquisition and lowered transport preserve packaging
construction: A wide compliant four-bar feeds a lowered second stage and a fixed-heading adjustable-hood launcher. The compact climb replaces an earlier size-constrained concept. A central transport feature remains from a dual-intake idea that was not built.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly wants the collector to collapse in wall contact, especially behind the hub where visibility is poor; climb packaging motivated the alternate arrangement.
engineering_analysis: A visible legacy feature is not proof of a fielded subsystem. Collector compliance must work with the pneumatic state and hard stops, while a lower transport path can alter compression and dead zones.
recommended_validation: Test blind-side contact, full-path flow and climb/shooter clearance; retain the unbuilt dual-intake status.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A fast rejected climb is not the same as a useful fielded climb
construction: A nonparallel four-bar and passive bumper-gap flap feed a ramp and turreted launcher with added brass inertia. The team says a faster two-arm climb had mechanical problems, so it reverted and widened hooks to clear the turret/reduce swing.
team_stated_reason: The source explicitly prioritizes the revised reliable climb over the failed fast alternative.
engineering_analysis: Useful timing includes completion probability and physical interference. A turret that scores well can still block the climb’s swept envelope. Continuous wheel idling also has an electrical/thermal cost that should be measured.
recommended_validation: Test hook clearance over turret range, climb swing and repeated-volley wheel recovery.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: Dual acquisition improves route flexibility without proving every component optimal
construction: A second opposed collector was added after the single-intake early robot to support drive-by autonomous pickup. The source reports wide mecanum collectors, a controlled upward/passthrough belt path and a later moving-shot solution. The onseason climb differs from an offseason traversal upgrade.
team_stated_reason: The team explicitly ties dual pickup to easier drive-by autonomous, while cautioning that its mecanum implementation required many iterations and was not a blanket recommendation.
engineering_analysis: A successful robot can contain a mechanism the team would not copy again. Preserve that negative experience. Additional pickup directions buy route freedom, but require two transport-entry cases and greater repair exposure.
recommended_validation: Compare complete auto routes, feed/rejection recovery and the exact onseason climb; do not back-project the offseason improvement.
limitations: Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

title: A six-bar collector and configurable CAD need version-aware interpretation
construction: The reveal describes a six-bar pickup with knockdown rollers for bouncing cargo, adjustable launcher rails/top roller and traversal climb. The later CAD release explicitly includes a configuration for the original Glacier Peak climb.
team_stated_reason: The stated roller purpose is controlling bouncing balls and the rail/top-contact purpose includes a broad shooting envelope with reduced unwanted spin. Exact design-choice causation beyond that is not established.
engineering_analysis: A configurable assembly can preserve genuine history, but the default displayed CAD is not automatically the configuration used at every event. Knockdown and acquisition contacts should be tested together; a roller that stops bounce may also create a pinch.
recommended_validation: Inspect both CAD configurations and validate bouncing-entry behavior plus disabled climb retention.
limitations: First-party release topics 404720 and 412974; no technical-video rewatch claimed. Reveal text and topic title use differing names, so source naming is preserved rather than silently harmonized.
